content: Yale-New Haven Hospital, commonly referred to as YNHH, is a prestigious 944-bed medical facility located in downtown New Haven, Connecticut. It operates under the ownership of the Yale New Haven Health System, Inc. The hospital encompasses the 201-bed Yale-New Haven Children's Hospital and the 76-bed Yale-New Haven Psychiatric Hospital. It serves as the primary teaching hospital for the Yale University School of Medicine. YNHH is consistently ranked among the top hospitals in the United States and is accredited by the Joint Commission on the Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations (JCAHO). In 2007, U.S. News & World Report ranked it as the 15th-best hospital out of 5,462 medical centers nationwide. The hospital was recognized for excellence in 10 of 16 evaluated medical specialties, including oncology, gastroenterology, otolaryngology, endocrinology, gynecology, cardiology and cardiac surgery, nephrology, psychiatry, pulmonology, and urology. Its geriatrics and psychiatry departments are ranked among the top 10 in the nation, while specialties such as gynecology, digestive disorders, endocrinology, nephrology, pulmonology, and oncology are ranked in the top 25. Annually, the hospital manages over 503,000 outpatient and emergency visits and approximately 50,000 inpatient discharges. YNHH is the second-largest employer in New Haven, with a workforce of about 6,000 employees and a medical staff of over 2,200 physicians specializing in more than 100 fields. The origins of Yale-New Haven Hospital date back to 1826, when the General Hospital Society of Connecticut was established as the first hospital in the state and the fourth voluntary hospital in the United States. Initially operating out of temporary facilities, the hospital raised $5,000 to purchase land and construct a permanent building. In 1833, a 13-bed hospital was opened on a 7.5-acre site bordered by Cedar Street, Howard Avenue, Davenport Avenue, and Congress Avenue. The original structure, known as the State Hospital, was designed by prominent New Haven architect Ithiel Town and cost $13,000. During the American Civil War in 1862, the hospital was converted into a military facility named the Knight United States Army General Hospital, in honor of Jonathan Knight, the president of the board of trustees. Civilian patients were temporarily relocated to Whitney Avenue. After the war, the hospital reverted to civilian use in 1865 and resumed its original name, State Hospital. In 1873, the hospital established the Connecticut Training School, the third nursing training program in the United States. In 1884, the institution was renamed New Haven Hospital to reflect the name commonly used by local residents. A formal affiliation with the Yale School of Medicine was established in 1913, marking the beginning of the Yale-New Haven Medical Center. In 1914, the hospital acquired its first motorized ambulance. In 1945, it was renamed Grace-New Haven Hospital following an affiliation with Grace Hospital. The New Haven Dispensary, the city’s first outpatient clinic established in 1871, merged with Grace-New Haven Hospital in 1951. A more formal agreement with the Yale School of Medicine in 1965 led to the hospital being renamed Yale-New Haven Hospital. In 1993, the Yale-New Haven Children's Hospital was opened, becoming Connecticut's first full-service pediatric hospital, including the state’s first dedicated pediatric emergency department. The Yale-New Haven Psychiatric Hospital was established in 2000 following the acquisition of the Yale Psychiatric Institute. Today, YNHH is a 944-bed private, nonprofit institution recognized as one of the nation’s leading medical centers. It is the largest provider of acute care in southern Connecticut and serves as a major referral center for the Northeast. The main campus of Yale-New Haven Hospital consists of three interconnected inpatient pavilions, bounded by South Frontage Road, Park Street, Howard Avenue, and York Street. The East Pavilion, originally called the Memorial Unit, was opened in 1950 and designed by architect Douglas Orr. The South Pavilion followed in 1982, and the West Pavilion, housing the Yale-New Haven Children's Hospital, was completed in 1993. These pavilions are connected by a central atrium. In 2000, the hospital acquired the nearby Yale Psychiatric Institute, designed by architect Frank Gehry in 1989, and converted it into the Yale-New Haven Psychiatric Hospital. In 2004, the Yale-New Haven Shoreline Medical Center in Guilford, Connecticut, was opened. The New Haven Pavilion, located across the street from the inpatient pavilions, houses outpatient clinics, clinical laboratories, and administrative offices. This pavilion occupies the site of the original hospital built in 1833 and connects directly to the Yale School of Medicine. Including outpatient and primary care facilities, as well as administrative offices, the hospital spans 1.9 million square feet, with ongoing expansion. In 2004, Yale-New Haven Hospital proposed the construction of a new $430 million building for the Yale Cancer Center, a Comprehensive Cancer Center. Although construction was initially scheduled to begin in September 2005, it was delayed due to disputes with unions and the city. An agreement was reached on March 22, 2006, and construction commenced on May 18, 2006, with the demolition of the Grace Building and site preparation. Groundbreaking for the new facility, known as the North Pavilion, took place on September 6, 2006. The building, which will connect to existing facilities via the atrium, is scheduled to open in 2009. Yale-New Haven Hospital has achieved numerous medical milestones, including the first X-ray in the U.S. (1896), the first successful clinical use of penicillin (1942), the first use of chemotherapy for cancer (1942), and the development of the first artificial heart pump (1949). It was the first U.S. hospital to allow healthy newborns to stay in rooms with their mothers (1946) and introduced natural childbirth (1949). The hospital has been a pioneer in organ transplantation, performing Connecticut’s first kidney transplant (1967), liver transplant (1983), heart transplant (1984), and pancreas transplant (1989). It was also the first in New England to achieve an in vitro fertilization birth (1983). Other notable achievements include the identification and naming of Lyme disease (1975), the development of the first insulin infusion pump for diabetics (1978), and the establishment of the first AIDS clinic in Connecticut (1982). The hospital has also been at the forefront of cancer treatment, introducing the first linear accelerator for cancer therapy in Connecticut (1963) and the first hospital-based comprehensive newborn screening program for sickle cell anemia in the U.S. (1972).
